title: Challenging Diagnosis of Fahr's Disease Mimicking Parkinson's Disease: A Case Report
case_prompt:
A 57‐year‐old man presented with a 20‐year history of progressive neuropsychiatric and motor symptoms. His symptoms began at age 37 with right leg numbness and gait disturbances that gradually worsened over 2 years, eventually requiring assistance with daily activities. He reported no substance use. Family history was notable for his mother with obsessive‐compulsive disorder, a sister with infantile seizures and borderline intelligence, and an uncle with rapid neuropsychiatric decline.

On examination, he had mild impairment in attention and concentration but was fully oriented. His gait was slow and shuffling without spasticity or ataxia. He demonstrated severe motor slowness, markedly reduced gait velocity, and pronounced bradykinesia. His voice was very soft with low pitch and resonance. Neuropsychiatric features included depressed mood, abulia, anhedonia, paranoid ideation, psychomotor retardation, visual hallucinations of shadows, obsessive thoughts about cleanliness, and frequent headaches. Mental status showed poor eye contact, masked facial expression, a stooped posture, restricted affect, impaired short‐term recall, reduced concentration, and partial insight.

He was initially diagnosed with early‐onset Parkinson’s disease and treated with Levodopa and Amantadine, but his motor and psychiatric symptoms showed minimal improvement over several follow‐up visits. Neurological examination revealed rigidity, reduced arm swing, a positive glabella tap, and no tremor or dystonia. An electroencephalogram was unremarkable.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Early‐onset Parkinson’s disease was considered because of adult‐onset parkinsonian signs before age 50 — “This manifestation was characteristic of Parkinsonian syndromes, prompting an initial diagnosis and treatment for EOPD.”  
2. Schizophrenia was evaluated given the patient’s psychotic features but ruled out by psychiatric criteria — “The patient was also evaluated for schizophrenia based on DSM‐5 criteria, which did not support the diagnosis.”  
3. Cysticercosis was considered as a cause of basal ganglia calcification but excluded by history and specialist review — “The major differential diagnoses for secondary causes of brain calcification, including cysticercosis… were systematically excluded through detailed clinical history, and multidisciplinary consultations with infectious disease specialists, internists, and neurologists.”  
4. Lead toxicity was considered and ruled out by the same multidisciplinary assessment — “The major differential diagnoses for secondary causes of brain calcification, including… lead toxicity… were systematically excluded through detailed clinical history…”  
5. Hyperparathyroidism was considered and excluded by normal metabolic panels — “The major differential diagnoses for secondary causes of brain calcification, including… hyperparathyroidism… were systematically excluded…”  
6. Manganese toxicity was considered and ruled out via clinical and laboratory evaluation — “The major differential diagnoses for secondary causes of brain calcification, including… manganese toxicity… were systematically excluded…”  
7. Wilson’s disease was considered and excluded through clinical evaluation and specialist input — “The major differential diagnoses for secondary causes of brain calcification, including… Wilson’s disease, were systematically excluded…”
